newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German jobless surges to new post-war record.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German jobless surges to new post-war record.

text.p: German unemployment surged by over a half a million to a new post-war record of 4.66 million in January, the Federal Labour Office said on Thursday.
The unemployment rate, which is based on unadjusted data, rose to 12.2 percent, compared with 10.8 percent in December.

On a seasonally adjusted basis the number of unemployed workers rose by 160,000 from December to 4.317 million in January -- smashing average expectations among economists polled by Reuters of a 52,000 rise.
Federal Labour Office chief Bernhard Jagoda said that the number, while serious, was affected by bad weather and he predicted that more Germans would get back to work this spring.

"This figure cannot be made to look good, but it should also be recognised that the situation in January contains seasonal unemployment, and it follows that in spring we can reckon with a clear reduction," Jagoda told reporters.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, speaking at a meeting of his Christian Social Union (CSU) in Munich, called unemployment Germany's "gravest problem", making planned tax and social security reforms more urgent than ever.
The increase, boosted by bad weather that idled large numbers of construction workers, came as a major surprise to independent analysts.

"The numbers show a structural rise in unemployment which is very worrying," Armin Kayser at SBC Warburg said. "Germany currently lacks the growth momentum which is necessary to stabilise the labour market."

The sharp rise also threatens Germany's drive to contain its deficit to qualify this year for European monetary union, as its state finances based on the assumption of stable unemployment, the analysts said.
"There is a high risk Germany will not meet the three percent gross domestic product-to-defict ratio target of the Maastricht Treaty," said Joerg Kraemer, a Merrill Lynch economist in Frankfurt.

Kraemer as well as other analysts said the jobless rise should increase pressure on the Bundesbank to cut interest rates to lift the economy, although few expected the central bank to do so at its meeting on Thursday.
"I think they will hold rates today, but rates should go lower," said Nick Stamenkovic of DKB International in London.
In western Germany, the number of people out of work on a seasonally adjusted basis rose to 3.029 million in January from 2.951 million the month before.
In eastern Germany, the number rose on an unadjusted basis to 1.288 million from 1.207 million in December.
